description: We are a team of students from Politecnico di Milano with a shared passion for space exploration and computer science. Our backgrounds combine aerospace and mechanical engineering with programming and data processing in Python, MATLAB and web development. We are building ByteTheMoon – Lunar Landing Site Navigator, an interactive 3D tool that turns NASA and ESA data into clear, comparable landing-site maps.
summary: Byte the Moon is an interactive 3D tool for lunar landing site analysis, for students and technical users. It uses NASA data to rate sites depending on different parameters.
details:
The analysis starts from NASA LOLA elevation data. For each point, a local plane is fitted through the point and its neighbours using a Python script to compute slopes across the entire Moon, classifying them as green, yellow, or red. Earth visibility is calculated in Python using JPL Horizons ephemerides by tracking Earth’s elevation above the local horizon over time while accounting for surrounding terrain obstructions. Communications are evaluated via a direct-to-Earth link (without relay satellites) by computing the received signal power at the three DSN complexes in Goldstone, Madrid, and Canberra.

To ensure high scientific fidelity, the environmental and resource layers integrate established space frameworks and datasets. Radiation and surface charging are modelled using ESA’s SPENVIS, with MATLAB used to collect charging potential data for Python processing. Illumination and solar power generation are derived from the Sun’s position using JPL Horizons ephemerides. Surface temperatures are modelled based on the thermophysical framework established by Hayne et al. Water-ice deposits and lunar pits are identified using data products from LROC (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera).

Each criterion is evaluated against predefined thresholds (good, acceptable, or critical) that can be modified directly in the application to reflect the actual operational limits of different rovers and landers. Individual metrics are combined into an overall landing score. If any parameter falls within its critical range, the site is flagged as infeasible and the failing criterion is identified, while all other scores remain visible.

Developed using CesiumJS and Vite, the web application renders the lunar surface as an interactive 3D globe where each analytical layer can be independently enabled or disabled. What makes The Navigator creative is its unique ability to transform complex, multi-disciplinary orbital and environmental datasets into a real-time, customizable decision-making sandbox. By unifying terrain, communications, space weather, and in-situ resources into a single tool, it bridges the gap between mission-design trade-offs for engineers and hands-on exploration for students and the general public.
